What's New Around Georgetown This Summer: A Local's Field Guide

Last July, if you told a Georgetown neighbor you were meeting friends "downtown," the answer was almost always the same short list of Square regulars. This July, the answer depends entirely on which side of I-35 you live on. Three separate corridors have added serious weight to the local map in the past six months, and each one is pulling residents in a different direction.

That is the through-line worth noticing. The 2026 opening wave is not scattered. It is clustering on the Square, along West University near Wolf Ranch, and up at Rivery, and the corridor closest to your driveway is quietly reshaping what a normal Saturday looks like.

The three corridors, briefly

Think of Georgetown right now as a triangle. The Square anchors the south point, West University and Wolf Ranch anchor the west, and Rivery plus the incoming Junction anchor the north. Everything opening this year lands somewhere inside those three points. If you have been feeling like the town got bigger without getting further away, that is why.

The Square is quietly repositioning as an evening destination

For most of the last decade, the Square drew its energy from daytime foot traffic: coffee, boutiques, the courthouse lawn, the occasional festival. The 2026 openings tilt the balance toward dinner and drinks.

The Thirsty Longhorn is a sports tavern serving stadium-style food with a full bar, taking over the space previously occupied by The Palomino, and opened August 22. A block away, Juniper Cocktails & Kitchen leans upscale, with a menu built around a prime tenderloin with Robuchon potatoes and the house Juniper old fashioned. Together they cover both ends of the evening spectrum without either one having to be everything to everyone.

The longer-running anchors are shifting too. Juliet Italian Kitchen is celebrating ten years in business under new leadership, with CEO Timothy Rucker joining in May and two new executive chefs on the line. A menu refresh at a ten-year-old restaurant is a different signal than a new opening. It says the operators believe the Square has another decade of upside worth investing in.

Add the theater programming. Georgetown Palace Theatre's 2026 season includes performances of "Oklahoma!" and "Jesus Christ Superstar," which fills the calendar with reasons to walk from a Square dinner to a curtain call in one evening.

If you have not been to the Square after 7 p.m. on a weekend since spring, you are working with an outdated mental map.

West University is where the everyday errands got upgraded

The West University corridor from I-35 out to Wolf Ranch has been the quieter story, but it is arguably the one that will change more routines. This is where families end up on weeknights, and the 2026 lineup is stacked with fast, casual, and functional additions.

Playa Bowls opened at Wolf Ranch on Sunday, June 29, adding an açaí and smoothie option to a shopping center that has been thin on breakfast alternatives. A short drive west, HomeGoods opened at Cedar Breaks West Shopping Center on April 23, 2026, giving residents on the west side a home décor stop that previously required a Round Rock trip.

The bigger pins are still landing. Shake Shack is transforming a 3,000-square-foot space at 1320 W University Ave with an ETA of late June 2026, after construction started March 2. Texas Roadhouse has begun ground-up construction on its first Georgetown location at 2209 North Interstate 35, with an ETA of late September 2026. And Velvet Taco, the Dallas-founded fast-casual chain with 49 locations across eight states, is opening in the Bluebonnet Plaza strip mall on West University Avenue next summer.

Two smaller openings worth putting on the calendar: Birds Barbershop, the locally founded Austin chain with nine locations, is opening at 1310 West University Avenue in August, offering cuts for men, women, and children plus coloring services, and La Vaquerita Creamery is now open in Georgetown, owned by Yozue De, serving fresh Mexican ice cream and snacks year-round.

The pattern here is not glamour. It is convenience density. Enough is opening within a two-mile radius that a Saturday morning of errands no longer needs to cross I-35 twice.

Rivery is going from "that hotel area" to a full dining and entertainment node

For years, Rivery Boulevard read as a hotel and office pocket with a handful of restaurants attached. That is changing fast, and it is the corridor where a resident who has not been paying attention is most likely to feel behind by fall.

The near-term headliner: Sovian Restaurant & Cocktail Lounge, a European-inspired steakhouse blending French and Italian influences, opened at 1500 Rivery Blvd., Ste. 2175. The menu focuses on premium steaks, seafood, and classic European dishes with modern twists, in a 5,000-square-foot space that blends French and Italian design elements. It is the kind of room Georgetown has historically driven to Austin to find.

The larger shift is still under construction. The Junction Entertainment District opens in Georgetown in summer 2026, bringing nearly 60,000 square feet of food, drink, live music, and recreation, anchored by a fully leased roster of restaurants that signed on before construction even began. Early coverage from outlets like the Texas Real Estate Research Center has underscored just how unusual that scale is for a suburban project, describing it as the first true entertainment district north of the city designed from scratch rather than retrofitted into existing buildings.

That last detail is the one to sit with. A 60,000-square-foot ground-up entertainment district is not a strip center with a food hall bolted on. It is a purpose-built venue with the kind of infrastructure that pulls people from Round Rock and Liberty Hill in for the weekend, not the other way around.

When it hits 100° and you want to stay close

The new openings get the headlines, but the summer routine most Georgetown families actually run is built around free stuff outdoors. A few reminders worth pinning to the fridge.

The splash pad at San Gabriel Park and the play areas at Garey Park handle the "we need to burn energy" hours, both connect to nature trails, and the Sunset Movie Series runs free outdoor films during the summer months. Between those and the Palace Theatre indoor programming, the local weekend can stay entirely inside Georgetown city limits from June through August without repeating itself.

One footnote that is easy to miss: the Friends of Georgetown Parks and Recreation, the nonprofit that supports the parks system, received $1.2 million from the first Two Step Inn, $1.1 million from the second, and $1.2 million from the third, funding an outdoor movie screen and $50,000 in scholarships for Georgetown residents in 2025. The music festival most residents mainly notice for the road closures is quietly paying for the summer amenities their kids use in July.

What all of this actually means

Pull back and the picture is straightforward. Georgetown in the summer of 2026 has three distinct nodes doing three distinct jobs. The Square is becoming a real evening scene. West University is compressing errands and family dining into a tighter footprint. Rivery is stepping into a lane the city has never really had, with Sovian open now and The Junction landing before fall.

For anyone who has lived here through the last five years of "coming soon" signs, this is the summer the signs come down.
